summary: Redwood AE + SE walked NexWave Health through the Console tracing, error analysis, and request logs debugging flows. Customer wanted to understand how tracing ties to request logs and how to surface root causes for generation errors and latency spikes. Discussed hosted vs Dedicated tradeoffs, VPC/KMS requirements, and next steps to run a pilot and share security docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya with Redwood, and with me is Liam, our SE. Quick intros?
[00:10] Sara (NexWave CTO): Hi all, Sara here - CTO at NexWave Health. We're looking at Redwood for inference infra, mainly to reduce latency and get better debugging tools.
[00:18] Rajiv (NexWave): Rajiv, lead ML eng. We handle model ops and want to understand tracing and error analysis.
[00:23] Tina (NexWave): Tina, DevOps - I'll own the VPC/KMS questions.
[00:28] Liam (Redwood SE): Great, thanks. Today we'll demo the Console tracing flows: how traces map to request logs, how to jump from an error observed in the application to the exact token and kernel execution path. We'll also show request logs, raw payloads, and how to set retention and RBAC for logs.
[00:44] Maya: Quick note — we'll be a little informal, so feel free to interrupt. We'll also capture next steps at the end.
[01:02] Liam: Starting the Console — top left is the tracing tab. You can search by request_id, model, or route. I'm going to filter to their demo dataset, "nexwave-demo", to show an example error.
[01:28] Liam: Here you see a trace with a 1200 ms tail latency spike and an associated error: "kv cache miss caused OOM" — sometimes auto-transcription shows K-V cache as K V cach in our logs, so ignore capitalization.
[01:46] Rajiv: Wait, OOM in trace? We thought OOMs only happened on Dedicated with big batches. Is this in hosted?
[01:55] Liam: Good question — this one is on a hosted instance with an optimized quantized model. The trace shows that a request attempted a large prefix which pushed the KV cache beyond threshold, we have heuristics to evict but in rare cases it triggers an error.
[02:18] Sara: How would we reproduce that locally? We have our own infra for some experiments.
[02:25] Liam: You can repro by sending the same request_id payload via our API with --request-id header; the Console has a "Replay" button which replays the exact payload against a sandbox model variant. I'll demo that.
[02:40] [03:05] Liam: (click) Replay captured request... replay starts... see the stepper on the right, it shows token generation timeline and kernel selection. The error reproduces in the replay — and Console surfaces the exact internal error message plus the stack of kernel calls.
[03:36] Tina: Can we redact PII in request logs? We can't send PHI to external services without redaction.
[03:44] Maya: Yes — for hosted we support automatic PII redaction rules (regex-based) and you can also enable client-side redaction with your SDK. For Private/Dedicated we support routing logs to your S3/GCS bucket or into your own SIEM via forwarders, so PHI never leaves your VPC.
[04:03] Rajiv: So for Private deployment we'd get full raw payloads but they stay in our VPC?
[04:09] Liam: Exactly. In Private mode the control plane can be customer-managed, and request logs can be configured to persist to your bucket and encrypted with your KMS key.
[04:20] Sara: How does tracing correlate to request logs? Like, how do we map a span to the raw payload?
[04:28] Liam: Every trace has a request_id which also indexes into the request logs. In the Console the trace view shows a "View Request" link which opens the raw payload, headers, and token-level timings. You can also export a combined JSON.
[04:45] [05:10] Liam: Here's an example: we open the request log, you can see prompt, system messages, streaming tokens, then an error at token 183. The error metadata includes runtime kernel name, device id, and memory snapshot.
[05:35] Rajiv: Memory snapshot — can we see memory pressure over time?
[05:40] Liam: Yes, we have a memory timeline for each trace; it shows GPU memory, CPU, and KV cache size. There's a heatmap view for heavy tail latencies.
[05:55] Tina: For compliance, we need audit logs of who viewed request logs. Does Console track that?
[06:02] Maya: We do. RBAC controls who can view request logs and every access is logged to an audit trail. For Dedicated/Private we can forward audit logs to your SIEM.
[06:15] Sara: Great. What about retention? We don't want to keep logs forever.
[06:20] Liam: Default retention is 30 days for hosted, configurable up to 90. For Dedicated and Private you control retention in your storage bucket.
[06:30] [07:05] Liam: Now switching to an error analysis flow: say you see a regression in quality — Console's error analysis links traces that have higher perplexity or hallucinations. You can group by prompt template, model version, or route.
[07:28] Rajiv: Do you run automatic checks to flag regressions?
[07:32] Liam: Yes, Optimize can run prompt-based evals and tie regression alerts to traces. We'll show a small example: a failing prompt set triggered an alert and Console listed top failing traces and sample tokens where the model diverged.
[07:52] Maya: We also support attaching test suites and can run them as part of CI to prevent rollouts that degrade quality.
[08:05] Tina: If we saw an error caused by a kernel bug, how flexible is the fallback?
[08:11] Liam: We have automatic fallback policies — you can route to a more conservative model variant or a lower-quantization variant. The tracing system shows which fallback triggered and why.
[08:27] Sara: For latency-sensitive endpoints, what are the knobs?
[08:32] Liam: Batching controls, max tokens, streaming thresholds. Console exposes batching windows and per-route SLOs; you can configure routing policies to prefer Dedicated capacity for SLO-critical routes.
[08:46] [09:15] Rajiv: Can we get token-level cost breakdowns in the trace?
[09:20] Liam: Yes — trace details include token counts, estimated compute cost, and which kernels were used, which helps optimize quantization vs latency tradeoffs.
[09:35] Alex (PM): Are there examples of companies using this for debugging production outages?
[09:40] Maya: Absolutely — we had a healthcare customer where tracing pointed to a specific prompt leading to KV growth, they adjusted prefixing and the error vanished. We can share a sanitized case study.
[09:55] Liam: I'm going to show how to create a saved view and alert: create an alert on error rate > 0.5% for route /inference/patient-notes — Console will email and push to Slack, and you can attach a presigned export of the top 10 traces.
[10:20] Tina: You mentioned presigned exports — how long are they valid?
[10:25] Liam: Configurable; default is 24 hours. You can lengthen for internal audits.
[10:30] [11:00] Rajiv: Networking: for VPC peering we need details on routing and port lists.
[11:06] Maya: We'll attach our VPC peering guide; top-level ports are 443 for control plane and gRPC ports for private datplane traffic — we'll send the exact list.
[11:20] Tina: KMS integration — does Redwood support customer-managed keys?
[11:25] Liam: Yes. For Dedicated and Private you can provide a KMS/HSM key and we encrypt request logs and runtime artifacts with it. For hosted we offer envelope encryption with BYOK options for enterprise tiers.
[11:40] Sara: What's the SLA for Dedicated?
[11:44] Maya: We have SLA-backed uptime and latency targets depending on the commitment level; we'll include the SLA doc.
[11:52] [12:30] Liam: Back to debugging flows — here's a live example of an error where tokenization mismatched the prompt encoding. You can jump from trace to the tokenizer diff view which shows how tokens were split and highlights where extra tokens were inserted.
[12:52] Rajiv: That would help us debug hallucinations caused by prompt engineering.
[12:56] Liam: Exactly. Also, Console can record a snapshot of model weights version, quantization profile, and patch level so you can exactly reproduce the environment.
[13:10] Maya: Quick pause — any questions so far?
[13:14] Sara: How long to onboard for Private?
[13:18] Maya: Typical timeline is 6–8 weeks for Private on a new VPC, faster if you already have a partner infra. Dedicated can be weeks depending on capacity allocation. We'll include an onboarding checklist.
[13:30] [14:05] Liam: Demoing the request logs export — I'm exporting a bundle that includes traces, request payloads, and the kernel execution logs. In the exported zip there's a CSV index and the full raw JSON per request.
[14:32] Tina: Are exports encrypted?
[14:35] Liam: Yes, encrypted in transit and at rest. For Private/Dedicated you can configure server-side encryption with your KMS key.
[14:46] Rajiv: Does the Console support queryable log storage (like ability to run SQL)?
[14:52] Liam: We index logs and provide a search DSL; for heavy querying customers often forward to their own log warehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake) via connectors.
[15:05] [16:00] Maya: We've been asked about retention and PI — we'll send standard SOW language and compliance docs.
[16:12] Sara: Can Redwood redact tokens that match PHI during streaming so they never appear in traces?
[16:18] Liam: We have streaming redaction hooks in the SDK; you can drop tokens client-side before they reach the API. We recommend defense-in-depth: client redaction + server-side rules.
[16:35] Tina: For our SOC2 audit we'll need proof of RBAC and audit trails.
[16:40] Maya: We'll provide audit log samples and the RBAC matrix.
[16:48] [18:00] Liam: Now I'm creating an alert template for dex-driven regression: add test set, set baseline, tie to rollouts — Console will block a rollout if metrics cross threshold.
[18:20] Rajiv: That ties into CI/CD?
[18:24] Liam: Yes, via our API you can trigger pre-deploy evals. We'll share example YAML for integration.
[18:40] [20:00] Maya: Wrapping up, recap — we'll send security docs, a recording of today's tracing walkthrough, Dedicated pricing tiers, and an onboarding checklist. Customer will share traffic profile and confirm pilot scope.
[20:20] Sara: Sounds good. Who's the primary contact?
[20:24] Maya: Me for commercial, Liam for technical.
[20:28] Alex: Can we get an example of a fallback policy config?
[20:32] Liam: I'll attach a snippet.
[20:36] Rajiv: One last question — in case of a production incident, what's the typical mean time to root cause with Console?
[20:42] Maya: Customers see root cause times drop from hours to under 30 minutes for token-level issues because traces point to the exact token and kernel. Of course it varies.
[20:55] Tina: Great. We'll review and follow up.
[21:02] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the items discussed.
[21:10] (end)
